title: Harbrook Bank: the fraud leak
prompt: Our client is Harbrook Bank, a large retail bank. Fraud losses on its card business have been climbing for three years, and the banking regulator has warned that it expects losses brought below a set threshold within two years. At the same time, the bank’s current fraud screening blocks a meaningful number of legitimate transactions, and cardholders are complaining. Management is evaluating a new machine-learning screening system and has asked us whether it is worth the money.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — Harbrook’s card business, annual figures
exhibits.unitsNote: A basis point (bp) is one hundredth of one percent

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — The cost of saying no
exhibits.text: Harbrook’s current screening declines 2% of all card transactions in error — legitimate purchases blocked as suspected fraud. The bank earns interchange of 1.5% on every transaction it approves, so each blocked purchase is revenue lost; declined cardholders also complain more and leave more often, which this case does not quantify.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — Proposed screening system, vendor terms
exhibits.unitsNote: Reductions are relative to today’s levels and assumed from the first year
exhibits.source: Vendor proposal, verified against reference banks

questions.prompt: Before we evaluate the system, what should we clarify with Harbrook first? Select the two most relevant.
options: How large are the fraud losses today, and what threshold has the regulator set?
Which advertising agency runs the bank’s card campaigns?
What does the current screening cost the bank beyond fraud itself — in blocked good transactions?
How many branches does Harbrook operate?
What colour are the bank’s credit cards?

optionRationale: The size of the problem and the bar the regulator has set are the two numbers the whole case is judged against.
Marketing has no bearing on screening economics.
The hidden half of the problem: screening has a false-positive cost, and any fix is judged on both sides of that trade-off.
Branch count does not bear on card fraud.
commonMistakes: Framing the case as fraud-only and missing that over-blocking is also a cost
Not pinning down the regulatory threshold that makes this urgent

questions.followUp:
Harbrook processes 500M card transactions a year at an average of $80 — about $40B of volume. Fraud losses currently run at 8 basis points of that volume; the regulator wants them below 5bp within two years.

And yes: the current screening also declines legitimate transactions in error. We will quantify that side too.

questions.prompt: Which areas would you investigate to decide whether the new system is worth buying? Select the four most relevant.
options: The annual cost of fraud today, and how much of it the system removes
The revenue lost to false declines today, and how much of it the system recovers
The full cost of the system — implementation and running
The compliance test: does the result get Harbrook under the regulator’s threshold?
Cafeteria costs at the bank’s head office

optionRationale: The headline benefit; without it there is no case.
The second benefit, and the one that makes this a customer-experience fix as well as a loss fix.
Benefits mean nothing until netted against what the system costs to buy and run.
Even a profitable system fails if it leaves Harbrook above 5bp — the regulator set a hard bar, not a preference.
Mortgages are a different book entirely.
Vendor diligence matters, but a biography is not one of the four analyses that decide this.
commonMistakes: Evaluating profit and forgetting the compliance test, or vice versa — this case has two pass/fail bars
Counting the benefits gross and skipping the running cost

questions.followUp: Let’s size the problem first. Here are the card business figures again — work from these.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, how much does card fraud cost Harbrook each year?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Volume: 500M transactions × $80 = $40B a year.
Fraud at 8bp: $40B × 0.0008 = $32M a year.
commonMistakes: Treating 8bp as 8% and answering $3.2B
Applying the rate to transaction count instead of volume
Slipping a factor of ten converting basis points

questions.followUp: $32M a year, and rising. Now the other leak — the good transactions the screening turns away. Here is what saying no costs.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, how much interchange revenue does Harbrook lose each year to falsely declined transactions?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Falsely declined: 2% × 500M = 10M transactions a year.
Blocked volume: 10M × $80 = $0.8B.
Forgone interchange: $0.8B × 1.5% = $12M a year.
commonMistakes: Counting the full $0.8B of blocked volume as the loss — the bank only earns the 1.5% interchange on it
Applying 2% to fraud losses instead of to all transactions
Ignoring this line entirely because it is not labelled "fraud"

questions.followUp:
So the screening problem costs $44M a year in total: $32M of fraud that gets through, plus $12M of good business turned away — before counting the customers who give up on the card altogether.

Here is the system the bank is evaluating.

questions.prompt: Using the vendor terms in Exhibit 3, what is the annual net benefit of the new system, once it is running?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, to one decimal place — for $15,700,000, type 15.7.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Fraud avoided: 60% × $32M = $19.2M a year.
Interchange recovered: 50% × $12M = $6M a year.
Gross benefit: $25.2M a year.
Less running cost: $25.2M − $10M = $15.2M a year.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the recovered interchange and netting only the fraud line
Subtracting the $20M one-off here — it belongs in the multi-year view, not the run-rate
Applying the 50% cut to fraud and the 60% cut to declines

questions.followUp: A $25.2M gross benefit against $10M of running cost — $15.2M a year net. Now put the one-off cost in and look at the full horizon.

questions.prompt: What is the net benefit of the system over five years, including the implementation cost?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Annual net benefit: $15.2M × 5 = $76M.
Less the one-off implementation: $76M − $20M = $56M.
commonMistakes: Charging the $20M every year
Using the $25.2M gross figure and forgetting the running cost
Stopping at the annual figure when the question asks for five years

questions.followUp: The system clears its costs comfortably — payback comes inside the second year. But profit was only one of the two bars. The regulator set the other.

questions.prompt: With the new system running, what would Harbrook’s fraud losses be as a share of card volume — and does that satisfy the regulator?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in basis points, to one decimal place — for 4.5bp, type 4.5.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Remaining fraud: 40% × $32M = $12.8M a year.
As a share of volume: $12.8M ÷ $40B = 3.2bp — comfortably below the regulator’s 5bp threshold.
commonMistakes: Cutting the 8bp rate by 50% instead of 60%
Dividing by transaction count rather than volume
Reporting the reduction (4.8bp) instead of what remains (3.2bp)

questions.followUp: So both bars are cleared: $56M of five-year value, and a fraud rate of 3.2bp against a 5bp requirement. Before we recommend, the risk function will ask what could go wrong with the system itself.

questions.prompt: What are the most relevant risks of relying on the new screening system? Select the three most relevant.
options: Model drift — fraudsters adapt, and a 60% reduction today may not hold next year
Integration risk — the system must sit inside payment flows that cannot go down
Governance risk — the regulator will ask how an ML model’s decisions are explained and audited

optionRationale: The central risk: fraud is an adversary, not a constant, and the business case assumes the reduction persists.
Real: screening sits in the authorisation path, and an outage there stops card payments, not just fraud checks.
Branches are not part of this case.
Real and specific to ML: a regulator that set a loss threshold will also expect the model to be explainable, monitored and challengeable.
commonMistakes: Treating the vendor’s reduction figures as permanent rather than a moving target
Missing model governance — a compliance case solved with a tool the regulator cannot audit is not solved

questions.followUp:
Model drift: agree performance floors in the vendor contract, monitor weekly, and keep an in-house challenger model.

Integration: run the system in shadow mode against live traffic before it takes decisions, with a kill-switch back to the current rules.

Governance: stand up model documentation, decision explainability and an audit trail from day one — take the regulator through it before go-live, not after.

questions.prompt: Harbrook’s Chief Risk Officer asks for your recommendation on the system. Please give your answer in seven to eight lines maximum.

keyPoints: Leads with the recommendation: buy and implement the system
Gives the compliance answer first — fraud falls from 8bp to 3.2bp, clearing the regulator’s 5bp bar with room
Gives the financial answer with numbers: $15.2M a year net, $56M over five years, payback inside two years
Notes the customer side: half the false declines disappear, which the complaint numbers will show
Names the conditions: shadow-mode rollout, contractual performance floors, and model governance the regulator can audit
Stays inside seven or eight lines
commonMistakes: Leading with the ROI and treating the regulatory requirement as a footnote — it is the reason the case exists
Presenting vendor reduction figures as certainties rather than contracted targets
Omitting the false-decline benefit, which is a third of the value

closing: That is the end of the case. Your transcript is ready — copy it into an LLM to be graded on what you actually said, not on what you meant.
